title: Western Ancestors, Part 1: Jiyu Kennet
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona will explore the teachings of Gyoku Carlson, an American Soto Zen abbot who emphasizes mindfulness and compassion, drawing on her lineage rooted in Eihei Dogen and his teachers. This lineage has evolved over centuries, from its origins in Japan to its spread throughout the West, influenced by key figures such as Roshi Juyukenet and D.T. Suzuki. Heigaku will delve into the history of Soto Zen, tracing its roots and evolution through texts like Keizan's Record of the Transmission of Light, which emphasizes the importance of koans in achieving enlightenment.
topics: Record of the Transmission of Light

sentences.text: Well, this evening's talk begins a series that will run from now through the end of practice period in March, on our Western ancestors.
These are the people who brought Soto Zen to North America, basically.
Before going that far back, I'm going to start a little closer and more current, with the Dharma Rain Sangha in Portland, Oregon, where Gyoku Carlson is the abbot.
She founded Dharma Rain with co-abbot Kyogen Carlson, who died last year.
Their teaching focuses, amazingly enough, on mindfulness and compassion, which feels familiar, with a focus on bringing those out of meditation and into daily life.
The few Dharma talks of hers that I listened to felt very familiar.
It feels like the same Zen that all of the other teachings we study are pointing to.
Gyoku Ko Carlson and Kyogen Carlson received transmission from the founder of Shasta Abbey.
That's in Mount Shasta, California, and it was founded as a continuation of the Soto lineage from Japan, but explicitly independent, not dependent on or a member of the Japanese hierarchy.
It was founded by Roshi Jiyu Kennet.
Roshi Jiyu Kennet lived from 1924 to 1996, and the focus of her teaching was on the stem of the Lotus Blossom.
We often talk about the Lotus Blossom as a symbol of Zen.
At the end of the meal chant, the Ino chants, "like a lotus in muddy water."
The concept is that Zen enables us to live in the muddy water of life, all the confusion, and still flourish like a lotus blossom.
Her tack was: sometimes that water is really turgid, really rough, really torrential, and so we have to make sure that the stem of the Lotus Blossom is strong enough to hold on.
Many people would describe her as a fierce woman.
She faced a lot of hardship on her Zen path.
Jiyu Kennet studied for eight years in Asia, mostly at Sojiji Temple in Japan, starting in 1962.

And unlike some of our neighboring priests who went young and inexperienced into Japanese residency, she did this after already being a lecturing member of the London Buddhist Society, having studied with D.T.
Suzuki, who is another Western ancestor that we'll probably talk more about.
Of course, he's different from our own Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, who founded the San Francisco Zen Center.
During those years in Japan, she faced illness and quite a bit of prejudice, especially at first, but worked through them with patience and persistence.
She writes:

*When I, like the untamed goose I was, set sail from England, I had a question to which I sought the answer, because that was the level of understanding at which I was then, and with which I must perforce start.
My question was a normal one for someone who had seen the bloodshed and cruelty of the Nazis in that last great and terrible war.
I thought my question was profound and meaningful.
I was that naive.
There will be many who will not consider my question to lack profundity, for I was asking why cruelty and death should exist.*
Interesting way to start, huh?
Why cruelty and death exist would be a naive question.
But she passes on the teaching that a teacher's duty is to help the student find the question behind the question behind the question, the real question embedded in the heart.
She found her ultimate question to be, "When was the first arising of selfishness?"
In other words, why is there death and cruelty in me?
She was eventually sanctioned, as I said, as the first woman to teach Soto Zen in the West, and she came to the United States to do that.
One characteristic of her teaching through the years is a struggle with the Japanese religious trappings, which probably sounds fairly familiar.
I've heard a lot of people in our group struggle with them.

Her struggle, however, was how to make the teaching appealing to the American audience without the Japanese religious trappings, and therefore how to replace them with Western Christian religious trappings, specifically making it in context for those of the Anglican experience.
So for example, in her translations, the pronouns for Buddha are always capitalized, "he" and "his."
She did spend some time with Shunryu Suzuki Roshi before going on to start that monastery at Mount Shasta.

One of her transmitted students, Reverend Sekai Lubke, argues that Jiyu Kennet went about founding a lineage differently from most of the other Western ancestors: she started a monastic practice from which grew a lay practice.
In most other cases the teachers worked with lay students, and those lay communities eventually decided to found a monastery.
That's the case with Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, who worked with lay students in France and San Francisco before founding the Zen Center and then Green Gulch and Tassajara.
Shasta Abbey does have a lay community and lay teaching, but it is not a strong or widely known one among those that have grown up in the United States.
We don't hear very much about it.
Lubke writes:
*The primary reason why Jiyu Kennet's disciples are a reclusive group of people is that we weren't taught to be teachers, we were taught to be monks.*
However, the basic manual of Zen, the primary book that Jiyu Kennet wrote, whose title changed from one edition to another, would be valuable to anyone who is ordained or a lay practitioner.
Her manual less conveys the attitude and perspective of Zen the way Suzuki Roshi's *Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind* does.

Her most recent title, *Zen Is Eternal Life*, which again gets back to that Anglican trapping, much more clearly lays out basic doctrines of the type that we discuss frequently here, such as the emptiness of self, causation, and the nature of suffering.

She does a particularly good job of distinguishing Mahayana Zen Buddhism from the elder Theravadan Zen Buddhism without dismissing the important contributions of the elder school, although she does use the pejorative term "Hinayana" to reference it, as was pretty standard for the time that it was written.
Finally, the book also contains translations of some important texts, some of our important scriptures, which I'll discuss more later.
At this point, a few weeks ago at Dave's Rohatsu ceremony, Tim passed on to him our lineage papers.
There were two of them, as Tim explained at the time.
There's the traditional men's lineage paper, and the women in our lineage had been largely omitted and erased.
So the modern women's lineage paper is under current reconstruction, through a bit of archaeology and study.
What we have up at the top here are just some little bits out of our lineage paper.
The men's lineage paper lists all of the men starting from Shakyamuni Buddha and going through, and in the women's lineage paper, they're in a circle.
I've got highlighted here some of the names that are part of this story we're about to go into.
Ironically, the name of the woman I want to talk about now is not in the current version of the women's lineage.
She is in some of the older versions, but as more people have been discovered, the criteria for getting on this list got a little more challenging.
We often talk about the founder of Soto Zen being Eihei Dogen, who lived from 1200 to 1253.
We often talk about his teacher Rujing: Dogen went to China, studied with Rujing, and then came back and founded the Eiheiji Temple.
We often don't talk about Dogen's other teacher Myozen, a Rinzai teacher that Dogen studied with before going to China.
But Myozen is also on our lineage paper.
I would like to go to Myochi, who is a crossroads, an intersection between these two lineages.
Myochi was a lay student of Myozen at the time that Dogen was, and also a major supporter of Myozen.
Then Dogen went to China and studied under Rujing, and when Dogen came back and founded Eiheiji, Myoji became a lay student of Dogen and a major financial supporter of Dogen.
Myochi was a [unclear: "egotie"] of Kannon, the Bodhisattva of Compassion.
She had a daughter, Ekan, who eventually became a nun and founded two temples, Hoji and Jojuji.
Ekan had a son who was Keizan.
Keizan is often referred to as the second founder of Soto Zen, and is the one who popularized Soto Zen, or is credited with popularizing it.
Dogen had established a firm school, but it wasn't widely recognized.
Keizan got monks to interact more with people outside of the monastery and go out and spread the word, spread the teaching.
Keizan founded two temples.
One is Sojiji, which is where Jiyu Kennet studied a thousand years later, almost 800 years later.
The other one is Yokoji, which I've got down here, but it should actually be up under Keizan.
I'll get to that in a bit, why it's down there.
In his autobiography, Keizan strongly credits his mother and his grandmother for their influence on his understanding of Zen.
So Miyoichi and Ekan continued to influence his understanding throughout his teaching, and when he got power and got [unclear: "kaki"], they would firmly and gently bring him down a bit.
Now, modern author Sallie Tisdale is a senior lay and trusted teacher at Dharma Rain, studying under Gyokuko Carlson, who studied under Jiyu Kennet.
In her book, *Women of the Way*, she takes the story from there.
I'm going to read a bit from the story where we are, after crossing through Miyoichi and Ekan and Keizan.
*While still living at Daijoji,* which I think is Sojiji, *Keizan met Mokufu Sone.
Her name was subtle and intricate.
It meant ordered silence and enduring ancestor and many other things.
In 1312, she donated a large amount of land in a place called Tokoku and asked Keizan to build a temple there.
It was a long way in more than miles from Kyokoku to Yokoji.

One traveled north and a little west, up toward a peninsula jutting out into the cold, rough sea, with range after range of mountains covered in evergreen and broken by emerald rice paddies in the lowlands, where white egrets bogged their heads among silvery shoots.
The weather was difficult.
Typhoons in the summer, blizzards in the winter, and rain the rest of the time.

Nevertheless, the land was beautiful, azure, and rich, thick with bamboo and cypress, grasses and ferns and wildflowers, cedars and misty fogs, and always a gray sea, sharp rocks jutting out of the breaking waves like the old ink washes of the Chinese painters.*
*The clouds were thick and low and close at times, knocking into the hills and trees, the sky constantly shattering and being remade, dark, blue, implacable, alive.
One night, Keizan dreamed that his grandmother, Miyoji, had come to him and asked to be ordained.
The next day, Sonin, who was still very young, invited Keizan to engage in Dharma combat with her, the spirited, metaphor-laden interview testing a student's understanding.
Keizan asked Sonin, "The year is almost gone, and another new year will come.
So how about your religious life?"
Sonin answered, "In the branches of the tree without shadow, is there any kind of time?"
Excellent.
Keizan was pleased.
Here was a person with a deep and earnest mind, with the flavor of the Dharma in her words.
Already he trusted her, already they were like master and disciple, as well as friends.
When she asked him to ordain her, he could not have been happier.
Because of his dream, he believed from then on that Sonin was his grandmother reborn.*
*In 1321, the Buddha Hall was built.
That season, a nun named Konto Ekyu arrived and immediately made herself at home, as though she had always lived there.
She began to organize the nuns and manage their work.
Month by month, season by season, more buildings and more altars were built, and more people came until dozens of monks and almost 30 nuns lived in the community.
The men and women sat together for morning services, then separated to do their work and study.*
So Ekyu became the first woman to receive transmission in the Soto lineage, and Sonin became the abbot of a convent at Yokoji.
Keizan's primary work is the *Record of the Transmission of Light*.
It's not a television.

Contrast that to the name *The Hidden Lamp*, the book of women's koans that we've talked about before, which I believe was originally titled something even close to that, something like *The Transmission of the Hidden Lamp*.
So this is a book of koans that tells the enlightenment story of the male line of ancestors from Buddha through Keizan's teacher.
The most common translation is this one, which you may have studied, by Thomas Cleary.
Thomas Cleary is certainly one of the most prolific translators of Zen material, of East Asian material.
His translations are often considered to be wise, but he often strays fairly far from the original text in order to convey his understanding.
So if you're interested in another translation, that can be found in Jiyu Kennet's Zen manual.
What is the title of Cleary, I can't quite see now?
*Transmission of Light*.
I'm going to jump, as an example, to Ananda's Enlightenment, which is a fairly well-known koan, in contrast to another well-known koan in the Gateless Gate, or the Mumonkan.
The first koan in that collection is Zhaozhou's dog.
You've probably heard of it: Zhaozhou received the question from a monk, "Does a dog have Buddha nature?"
And Zhaozhou responded, "Mu," which means absent.
Working with that koan is probably the most well-known koan practice.
We were sitting, breathing with absence and studying emptiness and recognizing that most of our assumptions on which we base our whole worldview are extremely tenuous.
But Ananda's koan can be a bit of an antidote to that if there's too much mu going on, as Ananda's koan is the koan of yes.
*Ananda asked Makakashio*, she uses the Japanese name, Makakashio, *"My dear senior, what did Shakyamuni transmit to you besides his case of gold brocade?"
Makakashio called "Ananda."
Ananda replied, "Yes."*
*Makakashio said, "Chop down the flagpole,"* which is what they did when you won a debate.
In other words, Ananda was enlightened.
So sitting with that koan is sitting with yes.
That was quite fruitful for me.
Under Tim's guidance, I spent a number of months with yes, which is an affirmation of this thought that arises that really shouldn't arise in my head: it's okay, it does, and it can.
Or this thing that's happening in my life: yes, this happens, and that's okay.
And this thing that happens in the world, which I don't like: yes, that's okay.
And yes, I'm going to do something about it at the right time when the opportunity arises.

Well, looking at the time, I'm just going to jump right into a closing quote from Yokoku Carlson from Dharma Rain on Keizan's commentary to that koan, which includes basically saying our scriptures aren't enough.
If you know the history, the story of Ananda, he had an understanding of the teachings of the scriptures, but he had not attained enlightenment.
That enlightenment is something else.
And Yokoku Carlson said:
*If you make an effort to be one with your delusion, inevitably you start thinking of yourself and your delusion and you start looking for them.
And immediately you have created this big gulf.
Here's the me.
Where is it?
How does it show up?
There's a phrase in Zen, putting a head on top of your head.
You confuse yourself.
You add on to what's already difficult enough.
There's no oneness.
There's no unity, because the effort itself is creating more distinction, more separateness.
And yet,*
and that's another common Zen teaching, might be worth studying, and yet, and yet, that diluted effort is important.
Thank you for joining me in the diluted effort.
